deep.reconstruction:
Setting. This is part of an algebraic (not Dirichlet-principle) construction of the elementary Abelian integrals on the curve f(x,y)=0. f has degree m in y, so the curve has m sheets over the x-line.

From the previous page: phi(x,y,xi,eta) is a rational function on the curve, defined as follows.
(1),(2) Near x=xi, on the branch with y=eta, its expansion starts with a term of degree -1. On the other branches over x=xi it starts above degree -1.
(3) At x=infinity every branch has the form (1/m)x^{-1} + lower terms.
In modern terms, phi dx is a differential of the third kind. It has residue +1 at the point P=(xi,eta) and residue -1/m at each of the m points over infinity: with t=1/x, (1/m)x^{-1}dx = -(1/m)dt/t. Its integral is Omega(x,y,xi,eta) = ∫phi dx.

The G/f' functions. G(x,y) is the most general polynomial (f' = df/dy) such that:
- at every finite point, the expansions of G/f' in powers of x-x0 start above degree -1;
- at infinity, all leading terms have degree < -1.
Then G/f' dx is an everywhere holomorphic differential, a differential of the first kind. G contains p arbitrary coefficients (p = genus; the page writes the index as rho). Hence, at the top of the page:
  G/f' = C_1 phi_1(x,y) + ... + C_rho phi_rho(x,y),
where phi_alpha dx is a basis of the first-kind differentials.

Main relation. 'Dies vorausgesetzt' (my reading), one always has
  d/dxi phi(x,y,xi,eta) - d/dx phi(xi,eta,x,y) = Sum_alpha [ phi_alpha(x,y) psi_alpha(xi,eta) - phi_alpha(xi,eta) psi_alpha(x,y) ].
The derivatives are total derivatives along the curve: d/dxi = ∂/∂xi + eta'(xi) ∂/∂eta.
The psi_1..psi_rho are again rational of the form G/f'. At every finite point their expansions start above degree -1; at infinity they may have poles. So psi_alpha dx are differentials of the second kind, regular at all finite points, with poles only over x=infinity.

Why the relation holds (my reconstruction):
- In the variable x, the first term has the double pole (x-xi)^{-2}, since d/dxi (x-xi)^{-1} = (x-xi)^{-2}.
- The second term, d/dx of phi(xi,eta,x,y) ~ (xi-x)^{-1}, gives the same (x-xi)^{-2}. So the singularity at P cancels.
- The left side is therefore, in (x,y), a second-kind integrand with no finite poles. It can be expanded in the phi_alpha(x,y) and in second-kind integrands with poles at infinity, with coefficients depending on (xi,eta).
- The left side is antisymmetric under (x,y)<->(xi,eta). After a suitable choice (normalization) of the psi_alpha, the bilinear antisymmetric form can be brought to the canonical shape shown. The right side is visibly antisymmetric, so the relation is consistent.

Definitions at the bottom of the page:
  omega(x,y)_alpha = ∫ phi_alpha dx (first kind),
  varpi(x,y)_alpha = ∫ psi_alpha dx (second kind, poles at infinity),
  Omega(x,y,xi,eta) = ∫ phi(x,y,xi,eta) dx (third kind).

Purpose (next page). Every Abelian integral ∫F(x,y)dx can be written uniquely as
  rational + Sum C_i Omega(x,y,xi_i,eta_i) + Sum c_alpha omega_alpha + Sum c_{rho+alpha} varpi_alpha.
That is the decomposition of Abelian integrals with 2p independent classes of first and second kind. The relation on this page is the 'interchange of argument and parameter' needed for the period relations and for theta-function theory.

Illustration (my own check). Take y^2 = 4x^3 - g2 x - g3, so m=2 and p=1. Choose:
  phi(x,y,xi,eta) = (y+eta)/(2y(x-xi)),
  phi_1 = 1/y,
  psi_1 = -x/y.
Then the left side equals (x-xi)/(y eta) = phi_1(x)psi_1(xi) - phi_1(xi)psi_1(x).
For a general cubic a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d the left side is a(x-xi)/(4 y eta).
errors: The relation is asserted ('hat man stets') without proof on this page. It holds only after a suitable normalization: phi(x,y,xi,eta) is fixed only up to adding Sum c_alpha(xi,eta) phi_alpha(x,y), and the psi_alpha must be chosen to match. Otherwise the right side is a general antisymmetric bilinear expression, not the canonical sum.
Index notation is inconsistent: psi(xi,eta)_alpha versus psi_alpha(x,y). The genus is called p on the previous page but rho here. These are cosmetic slips.

The condition on the psi_alpha at infinity is not stated. Poles there are implicitly allowed, which is necessary since otherwise the psi_alpha would be first-kind integrands. The finite-point condition reads, as far as legible, 'leading terms of degree higher than -1'.
In the first derivative, the denominator was corrected (an x crossed out, xi written). It must be read as the total derivative in xi along the curve, with eta = eta(xi).

results.what: Basis of first-kind integrands as G/f' with G an adjoint polynomial; the dimension equals the genus p.
results.modern_name: Holomorphic differentials via adjoint polynomials; dim H^0(K)=g

results.what: Third-kind integrand phi(x,y,xi,eta) with residue +1 at (xi,eta) and residue -1/m at each infinite point.
results.modern_name: Normalized differential of the third kind / elementary integral of the third kind

results.what: d/dxi phi(x,xi) - d/dx phi(xi,x) = Sum[phi_alpha(x)psi_alpha(xi) - phi_alpha(xi)psi_alpha(x)], with psi_alpha second-kind integrands having poles only at infinity.
results.modern_name: Weierstrass's fundamental relation (H-function relation); algebraic form of the interchange of argument and parameter / Riemann bilinear relation for the canonical bidifferential
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass (Berlin lectures from the 1860s/70s, Werke IV, 1902); transcendental interchange theorem for normalized third-kind integrals to Riemann 1857 (Legendre/Jacobi in the elliptic case)

results.what: Definition of omega_alpha, varpi_alpha, Omega preparing the decomposition of an arbitrary Abelian integral into rational part plus third-kind, p first-kind and p second-kind integrals (next page).
results.modern_name: Decomposition of Abelian integrals; dim H^1_dR = 2g

deep.surprise_reason: The interchange of parameter and argument is known from Riemann's 1857 paper in its transcendental, normalized form. What is notable is the purely algebraic formulation: rational phi, explicit second-kind psi_alpha with poles at infinity, and an antisymmetric bilinear sum. This is exactly the shape of Weierstrass's later 'Fundamentalrelation' for his H-function and is usually attributed to Weierstrass's lectures. It is a notable unpublished detail, but the conceptual content is close to known Riemann material, and the dating and authorship of the sheet should be confirmed.

checkable.sympy: x,xi,y,eta,g2,g3=symbols('x xi y eta g2 g3'); P=lambda t:4*t**3-g2*t-g3; Pp=lambda t:diff(P(t),t); phi=lambda X,Y,Xi,Eta:(Y+Eta)/(2*Y*(X-Xi)); A=diff(phi(x,y,xi,eta),xi)+diff(phi(x,y,xi,eta),eta)*Pp(xi)/(2*eta); B=diff(phi(xi,eta,x,y),x)+diff(phi(xi,eta,x,y),y)*Pp(x)/(2*y); expr=simplify((A-B).subs({y**2:P(x),eta**2:P(xi)})-(x-xi)/(y*eta)); expr
checkable.asserts: For y^2=4x^3-g2x-g3 with phi=(y+eta)/(2y(x-xi)), phi_1=1/y, psi_1=-x/y, the left side equals phi_1(x)psi_1(xi)-phi_1(xi)psi_1(x)=(x-xi)/(y*eta). If the y^2 substitution is not applied automatically, verify that the combined numerator reduces to 0 after the substitutions y^2=P(x), eta^2=P(xi).

checkable.asserts: Key identity behind the elliptic check (should print 0). It gives LHS = a(x-xi)/(4 y eta) for a general cubic, so the double pole at x=xi cancels and the remainder is a first-kind times second-kind antisymmetric combination.
At infinity (t=1/x) on each of the m=2 sheets, phi dx ~ (1/2)x^{-1}dx has residue -1/2, so the total residue -1 balances the +1 at (xi,eta). This matches condition (3), (1/m)x^{-1}.

transcription_corrections: 'Die Schlussfolgerung[?] hat man stets[?]' is more likely 'Dies vorausgesetzt hat man stets'.

'die Anfangsglieder stets vom Exponenten[?] von dem (-1)ten Grade[?] sind' is most likely 'die Anfangsglieder stets von höherem als dem (-1)ten Grade sind', parallel to the condition on G/f' on the previous page.
In the first derivative the denominator shows a crossed-out x replaced by xi: '∂/∂xi φ(x,y,ξ,η)'.
The upper summation index is written as a rho-like letter (ρ), corresponding to the p of the previous page.
The trailing mark after φ_ρ(x,y) in the first equation is a struck-through stray character, not part of the formula.
